screens.title: What are Secure Coding Practices?
screens.narratorSegment: Secure coding practices are concrete engineering habits and A P I choices that reduce the likelihood of vulnerabilities in application code. At their core, these practices include input validation, output encoding, using safe APIs like parameterized queries, handling errors without leaking secrets, and failing safely when unexpected conditions arise. A clear example: validating that a username contains only allowed characters and length prevents many injection attempts and downstream surprises. A common misconception is that security is only about authentication or network controls; in reality, attackers often target logic flaws or improper data handling inside the application itself. Secure coding is also different from security testing — it reduces the number of defects you must find with scanners. Practically, you should treat every external input as untrusted, choose libraries designed for safety, and prefer explicit encoding APIs over ad-hoc string manipulation. When teams adopt these practices early, the cost of fixing security bugs drops dramatically, and incidents become less likely. As you review code, ask: 'Is this input validated? Is output encoded for its context? Are we using an A P I that separates code from data?' Those three checks catch many common problems.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Secure coding is a set of practices—validate, encode, and use safe APIs—that prevent common application-level attacks.

content.html:
Core Concept
Secure coding practices
Practical habits to keep application code resilient against attackers.
  • Validate inputs: treat external data as untrusted and check format and length.
  • Encode outputs: escape characters before rendering in HTML, SQL or shell contexts.
  • Use safe APIs: parameterized queries and templating engines that auto-escape.
Key Takeaway

Adopt validate-encode-use patterns early to reduce the number of security defects needing later fixes.

Concrete example
A username input should be checked for allowed characters and length before being used in a database query or rendered back to a page.
Analogy
Think of input validation as a security gate: only known-good shapes are allowed through, and everything else is rejected or normalized.
Common mistake
Relying only on client-side checks or assuming libraries always sanitize inputs is unsafe. Always validate on the server and use proven APIs.

screens.title: SQL Injection — Vulnerable Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: S Q L injection happens when user-supplied data is mixed directly into S Q L commands so attackers can change the structure of queries. The vulnerable pattern is simple: build a query string using untrusted input, then execute it. For a concrete example, imagine a login endpoint that constructs a query by inserting the username and password into a template. An attacker can supply values like "admin' OR '1'='1" which change the WHERE clause logic and bypass authentication. A common misconception is that escaping quotes on the client is enough — it is not. Escaping must be handled by the database driver or by parameterization on the server. In practice you should send S Q L and data separately to the driver so the database treats user input strictly as data. This prevents any injected control characters from being interpreted as S Q L. When reviewing code, look for string formatting or concatenation that builds S Q L; flag it for replacement with parameterized query APIs. The immediate takeaway: any direct concatenation of user input into S Q L is high risk and must be refactored.

keyIdea.title: Vulnerability
keyIdea.text: Directly concatenating user input into SQL statements enables attackers to alter query logic and access data they shouldn't.

content.html:
Vulnerability Example
Vulnerable SQL pattern
This code concatenates user input directly into the SQL string, allowing structure to be changed by an attacker.
# Vulnerable SQL query (DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION)
def get_user_vulnerable(username):
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}';"
    # execute(query)  # attacker could pass: admin' OR '1'='1' --
    # resulting SQL: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' OR '1'='1';
Explainer bullets
  • Root cause: mixing code and data without a clear boundary.
  • Attack: craft input that injects SQL control tokens like OR, --, ;
  • Impact: data disclosure, modification, or complete compromise of the database.
  • Review tip: search for query string concatenation and f-strings used in SQL context.
Common Mistake

Relying on ad-hoc escaping is brittle. Use parameterized APIs supplied by the DB driver.

screens.title: Preventing SQL Injection — Parameterized Queries
screens.narratorSegment: The reliable defense against S Q L injection is parameterized queries. Instead of composing a S Q L string with user values embedded, send a statement with placeholders and pass user data as separate parameters to the database driver. The driver treats those values as data, not S Q L, so they cannot change query structure. For a practical Python example, use a placeholder like %s or? depending on the DB library, and pass a tuple or list of parameters. A misconception to watch for is thinking that escaping user input manually is equivalent; escaping is brittle and error-prone across different encodings and contexts. Parameterized queries centralize escaping to the driver with fewer mistakes. When refactoring, replace string concatenation with a parameterized execute call, and add automated tests that assert malicious inputs do not alter query results. The best practice is to also limit returned columns and privileges so even if logic errors occur, the blast radius is reduced. Preventing SQL Injection — Parameterized Queries means use parameterized queries provided by the database driver to separate code from data and prevent injection.. In practical terms, separate sql code from data so the database never treats input as executable sql. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Secure Fix
Parameterized queries
Send SQL and data separately so drivers never interpret user input as SQL.
# Secure SQL query using parameterized queries
def get_user_secure(username):
    query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s;"  # Placeholder
    # cursor.execute(query, (username,))  # Pass parameters separately
    # The database driver handles escaping and prevents injection.
Checklist for refactoring
  • Replace string concatenation with parameterized execute calls.
  • Limit query results and apply least privilege to DB user accounts.
  • Add tests that include malicious inputs to verify behavior.
Key Takeaway

Parameterization is the simplest, most reliable fix for SQL injection and should be the default pattern.

screens.title: OWASP Top 10 — A Practical Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: The OWASP Top 10 is a practical awareness document listing critical web application risks such as broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures, and security misconfiguration. Treat it as a prioritized checklist for design and code reviews rather than a strict taxonomy. In practice, use the Top 10 to create short review questions: 'Does this endpoint enforce authorization?' or 'Are we handling secrets and cryptography correctly?' A common mistake is using the Top 10 as the only security activity — it complements testing and secure development but does not replace threat modeling or secure configuration. To operationalize it, select one or two Top 10 items per sprint to monitor and add related automated tests or scanners. For example, pair dependency scanning with a focus on injection and cryptography in the next release. The Top 10 also helps communicate risk to non-engineers because each item maps to a concrete symptom or misconfiguration you can fix. Use it as a living checklist and update your internal templates to reflect the most relevant items for your application. screens.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Types
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-Site Scripting is a class of vulnerabilities where an attacker injects client-side scripts that run in other users' browsers. There are three practical types to know. Reflected XSS occurs when malicious input is immediately returned in a response without encoding — for example, a search page that echoes query parameters into the page. Stored XSS occurs when the malicious script is saved on the server, such as in a comment or profile field, and later served to many users. DOM-based XSS happens when client-side JavaScript reads fragments of the URL or other client-side data and dynamically inserts it into the document without encoding, so the browser executes it. A common misconception is that escaping once at input is enough; you must encode output for the specific context where it will be used (H T M L body, attribute, JavaScript, or URL). Practical defenses are input validation, context-aware output encoding, and using templating engines that auto-escape. When assessing risk, ask: 'Is untrusted data ever interpreted as H T M L or script by the browser?' If yes, treat it as high priority.

keyIdea.title: XSS types
keyIdea.text: Reflected: immediate echo; Stored: saved and served; DOM-based: client-side insertion — all require context-aware encoding to mitigate.

content.html:
Definition
XSS Types
Reflected XSS
Attacker input is immediately reflected in a page and executed.
Stored XSS
Malicious script is stored on server and delivered to many users later.
DOM-based XSS
Client-side code inserts untrusted data into the DOM, causing execution.
Defense checklist
  • Encode output for the correct context (HTML, attribute, JS).
  • Use templating engines that auto-escape by default.
  • Sanitize stored content when appropriate and apply CSP headers.
Common misconception
Client-side validation alone is insufficient because attackers can craft requests directly to the server.

screens.title: XSS — Unsafe Rendering and Safe Encoding
screens.narratorSegment: A concrete XSS example shows why rendering untrusted H T M L or using innerHTML/ document. write is dangerous. Suppose a page takes a name from the URL and writes it directly to the document, allowing an attacker to inject a script tag that runs in other users' browsers. The simple fix is to treat the value as text, not H T M L, using APIs that set text content, or use templating engines that escape H T M L. In the example provided, using textContent prevents the browser from interpreting H T M L tags. A trap to avoid is assuming URL encoding alone stops XSS — encoding must prevent the browser from parsing tags and event handlers in the rendered context. When you audit code, look for any direct insertion of untrusted strings into the document or innerHTML; those are high risk. The practical takeaway: always encode or use text-specific DOM APIs when inserting untrusted values into a page. Add a regression test that renders malicious payloads and asserts they appear as text, not executed script. XSS — Unsafe Rendering and Safe Encoding means use textcontent or templating engines that auto-escape to prevent injected scripts from executing in a browser.. In practical terms, an html/js example showing why textcontent matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe rendering
keyIdea.text: Use textContent or templating engines that auto-escape to prevent injected scripts from executing in a browser.

content.html:
Vulnerability & Fix
Unsafe document writing
<!-- Vulnerable HTML (DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION) -->
<p>Welcome, <script>document.write(decodeURIComponent(location.hash.substr(1)));</script></p>

<!-- Secure HTML (using proper encoding) -->
<p>Welcome, <span id="username"></span></p>
<script>
  const urlParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
  const username = urlParams.get('name');
  if (username) {
    // Use textContent to prevent HTML interpretation
    document.getElementById('username').textContent = username;
  }
</script>
Explainer
  • Why it fails: document.write interprets HTML and script tags as executable content.
  • Fix: insert text via textContent or let the template engine escape special characters.
  • Test: include a malicious payload in test input and assert it renders as text.
Key Takeaway

Always render untrusted strings as text and use context-aware escaping to stop XSS.

screens.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-Site Request Forgery tricks an authenticated user's browser into submitting unintended requests to a web application. The browser automatically attaches session cookies, so the server may accept the forged request as legitimate. A classic example is a malicious webpage embedding an auto-submitting form or an image tag that issues a state-changing POST to a bank transfer endpoint; if the victim is logged in, the transfer proceeds without explicit consent. The primary defense is a CSRF token: a unique, unpredictable secret generated by the server and included in each state-modifying form or request. When the server receives the request, it verifies the token matches the user's session. This prevents other sites from forging valid tokens. Another common mitigation is requiring same-site cookies or double-submit cookies, but tokens remain the most straightforward conceptual defense. A misconception is thinking that authenticated GET requests are safe; any state-changing action must require a protected token and use POST or other non-idempotent methods. When designing forms, include a server-generated token and verify it on submission. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) means use a server-generated, unpredictable csrf token in state-changing forms and verify it on the server to prevent forged requests.. In practical terms, how state-changing requests can be forged and the role of csrf tokens. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
Attackers trick a logged-in user into sending authenticated requests that the user did not intend.
Example form with CSRF token
<form action="/transfer" method="POST"> <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="100"> <input type="hidden" name="to_account" value="attacker_account"> <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{% csrf_token %}"> <!-- server-generated token --> <button type="submit">Transfer Money</button> </form>
Defence checklist
  • Include a server-generated token in forms and verify it on submission.
  • Use same-site cookie attributes where appropriate to reduce cross-site leakage.

CSRF tokens are a simple, effective guard against forged requests when properly implemented and verified.

screens.title: Secure Configuration and Dependency Scanning
screens.narratorSegment: Secure configuration management and dependency scanning are operational controls that complement secure coding. Start by eliminating default credentials, disabling unnecessary services, and applying least-privilege network and file permissions. For dependencies, enable automated scanning tools in CI to detect known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries. Tools will raise alerts for known CVEs and provide recommended upgrades. A practical process: track dependencies in a manifest, enable a scanner that opens PRs for fixes, and require a simple review step before merging. Don't ignore transitive dependencies either; scans that consider the full dependency tree are important. A common misconception is that running a scanner once is enough — you need continuous monitoring because new CVEs are discovered frequently. Also prioritize fixes: not all vulnerabilities are critical for your application. Use risk-based triage that considers exploitability and the data the component handles. Finally, ensure configuration is reproducible by codifying it (e. g., infrastructure as code) and testing non-default security settings in a staging environment before production rollout. Secure Configuration and Dependency Scanning means automate dependency scanning and enforce secure configurations to reduce exposure from libraries and infrastructure settings.. screens.title: Activity: Identify and Fix SQL Injection in Flask
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through a small Flask login endpoint that demonstrates S Q L injection in a realistic setting. The vulnerable code concatenates username and password into a S Q L string and executes it directly. To exploit it, an attacker can set the username to a payload like "admin' OR '1'='1' --" and any password; the WHERE condition becomes always-true and authentication is bypassed. The fix is to replace the vulnerable execute call with a parameterized query and pass the username and password as parameters to the database driver. When you refactor, test the endpoint with both normal credentials and malicious inputs; the secure version should never return a successful user unless credentials match. Also add unit tests that include malicious payloads to prevent regressions. A common misconception is to hide vulnerable code with scaffolding; instead, refactor the query and add tests and pipeline checks so the vulnerability cannot reappear unnoticed. This exercise shows how a few lines of change plus tests greatly reduce risk. Hands-on Activity
Find and fix the SQL injection in Flask
    # Vulnerable lines in the Flask app
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}';"
    user = conn.execute(query).fetchone()

    # Example attacker input to bypass:
    # username: admin' OR '1'='1' --
    # password: anything

    # Secure fix using parameterized queries
    query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?;"
    user = conn.execute(query, (username, password)).fetchone()
Review checklist
  • Pinpoint exact vulnerable lines that build SQL strings with user data.
  • Replace with driver parameterization and add tests with malicious inputs.
  • Run dependency scanner to ensure DB driver is up to date and supports parameterization safely.
Key Takeaway

A focused code change plus tests turns a critical vulnerability into a protected endpoint.

screens.title: Adopting a Security-First Mindset
screens.narratorSegment: Moving from knowledge to habit requires a security-first mindset. This means asking simple, repeatable questions during development and reviews: could this input be attacker-controlled, does this output reach a browser or other interpreter, and does this call use the safest available A P I? Start by baking security checks into the pull request template and code-review checklist so reviewers consistently check for validation, encoding, and parameterization. Add unit tests with adversarial inputs and include SAST in the pipeline to catch regressions. Another practice is threat modeling small changes — a two-minute mental model that identifies possible attacker goals and attack surfaces for the change. A common misconception is that security slows development; in fact, clear patterns and automation speed up safe delivery by preventing rework from late-stage bug fixes. Finally, pair programming or security-focused review rotations spread knowledge across the team and help teach junior engineers practical defensive patterns. The takeaway: turn security questions into lightweight rules and automated checks so safety becomes part of the development rhythm. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will treat security as a first-class part of coding. Secure coding practices mean writing software that anticipates attacker behavior, validates and encodes data, and resists common classes of exploits. You will learn why the OWASP Top 10 is a useful checklist for web application risks, and we'll walk through concrete examples of S Q L injection, Cross-Site Scripting, and Cross-Site Request Forgery. We will also cover secure configuration, dependency scanning, and how to adopt a security-first mindset in code reviews and CI pipelines. This matters because network controls and authentication are only one layer — remotely exploitable flaws in your application logic or unescaped inputs can still lead to data breaches, account compromise, or unauthorized actions. As you move through the screens, you will see vulnerable code patterns, practical fixes such as parameterized queries and output encoding, and a simple way to think about CSRF tokens. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions, like assuming client-side checks are enough or believing that libraries always protect you. By the end you should be able to recognize these vulnerabilities and take immediate steps to mitigate them in your projects. What will you change in your next code review?

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to recognize and remediate several classes of application-level vulnerabilities. First, you'll understand why secure coding is necessary through every stage of development and deployment, and how small mistakes in input handling or configuration lead to large breaches. Second, you'll learn to read and apply the OWASP Top 10 as a practical checklist during design reviews. Each objective includes a skill and why it matters: for example, being able to identify S Q L injection means you can find and replace unsafe string concatenation with parameterized queries, immediately reducing risk to customer data. You'll also practice spotting XSS and CSRF patterns and applying output encoding and token-based defenses. Finally, you will begin to incorporate dependency scanning and secure configuration checks into your build process. These skills reduce incident risk and make code reviews more effective. As you learn, try framing questions in reviews like: 'Could this input be controlled by an attacker?' or 'Does this response get rendered in a browser?', which leads directly to safer code.

This second objectives screen expands into practical abilities you will practice. You will learn to read code with a security lens: spot direct string concatenation to S Q L statements, detect unescaped user content rendered in H T M L, and notice missing anti-CSRF mechanisms in state-changing forms. We will walk through small code examples so you can both identify the flaw and suggest a specific fix. Another objective is to recognize when configuration or dependencies create risk: default credentials, open services, or outdated libraries with known CVEs increase attack surface. Finally, you will practice communicating security concerns in code review language — concise suggestions such as 'use parameterized query here' or 'escape user content before writing to document' are more actionable than vague warnings. These skills shorten the time from discovery to remediation and make security part of daily engineering practice rather than an afterthought. Try framing fixes as code changes and tests so they can be verified automatically.

Secure coding practices are concrete engineering habits and A P I choices that reduce the likelihood of vulnerabilities in application code. At their core, these practices include input validation, output encoding, using safe APIs like parameterized queries, handling errors without leaking secrets, and failing safely when unexpected conditions arise. A clear example: validating that a username contains only allowed characters and length prevents many injection attempts and downstream surprises. A common misconception is that security is only about authentication or network controls; in reality, attackers often target logic flaws or improper data handling inside the application itself. Secure coding is also different from security testing — it reduces the number of defects you must find with scanners. Practically, you should treat every external input as untrusted, choose libraries designed for safety, and prefer explicit encoding APIs over ad-hoc string manipulation. When teams adopt these practices early, the cost of fixing security bugs drops dramatically, and incidents become less likely. As you review code, ask: 'Is this input validated? Is output encoded for its context? Are we using an A P I that separates code from data?' Those three checks catch many common problems.

S Q L injection happens when user-supplied data is mixed directly into S Q L commands so attackers can change the structure of queries. The vulnerable pattern is simple: build a query string using untrusted input, then execute it. For a concrete example, imagine a login endpoint that constructs a query by inserting the username and password into a template. An attacker can supply values like "admin' OR '1'='1" which change the WHERE clause logic and bypass authentication. A common misconception is that escaping quotes on the client is enough — it is not. Escaping must be handled by the database driver or by parameterization on the server. In practice you should send S Q L and data separately to the driver so the database treats user input strictly as data. This prevents any injected control characters from being interpreted as S Q L. When reviewing code, look for string formatting or concatenation that builds S Q L; flag it for replacement with parameterized query APIs. The immediate takeaway: any direct concatenation of user input into S Q L is high risk and must be refactored.

The reliable defense against S Q L injection is parameterized queries. Instead of composing a S Q L string with user values embedded, send a statement with placeholders and pass user data as separate parameters to the database driver. The driver treats those values as data, not S Q L, so they cannot change query structure. For a practical Python example, use a placeholder like %s or? depending on the DB library, and pass a tuple or list of parameters. A misconception to watch for is thinking that escaping user input manually is equivalent; escaping is brittle and error-prone across different encodings and contexts. Parameterized queries centralize escaping to the driver with fewer mistakes. When refactoring, replace string concatenation with a parameterized execute call, and add automated tests that assert malicious inputs do not alter query results. The best practice is to also limit returned columns and privileges so even if logic errors occur, the blast radius is reduced. Preventing SQL Injection — Parameterized Queries means use parameterized queries provided by the database driver to separate code from data and prevent injection.. In practical terms, separate sql code from data so the database never treats input as executable sql. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cross-Site Scripting is a class of vulnerabilities where an attacker injects client-side scripts that run in other users' browsers. There are three practical types to know. Reflected XSS occurs when malicious input is immediately returned in a response without encoding — for example, a search page that echoes query parameters into the page. Stored XSS occurs when the malicious script is saved on the server, such as in a comment or profile field, and later served to many users. DOM-based XSS happens when client-side JavaScript reads fragments of the URL or other client-side data and dynamically inserts it into the document without encoding, so the browser executes it. A common misconception is that escaping once at input is enough; you must encode output for the specific context where it will be used (H T M L body, attribute, JavaScript, or URL). Practical defenses are input validation, context-aware output encoding, and using templating engines that auto-escape. When assessing risk, ask: 'Is untrusted data ever interpreted as H T M L or script by the browser?' If yes, treat it as high priority.

A concrete XSS example shows why rendering untrusted H T M L or using innerHTML/ document. write is dangerous. Suppose a page takes a name from the URL and writes it directly to the document, allowing an attacker to inject a script tag that runs in other users' browsers. The simple fix is to treat the value as text, not H T M L, using APIs that set text content, or use templating engines that escape H T M L. In the example provided, using textContent prevents the browser from interpreting H T M L tags. Let's summarize the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, the OWASP Top 10 is a practical awareness checklist that helps you prioritize common risks such as injection and misconfiguration. Second, S Q L injection occurs when user input changes the structure of a database query; the recommended fix is parameterized queries so the driver treats input strictly as data. Third, Cross-Site Scripting lets attackers inject client-side scripts; defend by encoding output for the correct context or using templating engines that auto-escape. These three concepts capture the most frequent and impactful application-level vulnerabilities you will encounter. Reflect on each term and ask: when was the last time I reviewed code for this specific class of problem? Turning that reflection into a checklist item for your next review increases the chance these issues are caught early. These are foundational and will help you triage risks quickly.

A few operational and pattern-based concepts round out your toolkit. Parameterized queries separate code from data and are the recommended defense against S Q L injection. Input validation and output encoding are complementary: validate inputs to reduce unexpected values and encode outputs for the exact context where data is rendered. CSRF tokens are the primary defense for preventing forged state-changing requests, and dependency scanning helps you catch known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries before they reach production. An important practical point is to combine these controls: parameterize queries, add encoding, include tokens for forms, and run automated scans in CI. A misconception is believing any single control is sufficient; layered defenses reduce the chance of a single point of failure. The final question to keep in mind is: which of these patterns can you automate or add to your team's checklist today to reduce the likelihood of a production incident?
